title: Core ideas in statistics
description: Read data honestly: averages, spread, chance, sampling and what evidence can show.

ideas.title: Center and spread
ideas.summary: A set of data is summed up by where its middle lies and by how far its values scatter around it.

items.q: In statistics, which measure of center is the middle value once the data are sorted?
items.a: The median

items.q: Why is the median often reported instead of the mean for incomes or house prices?
items.a: A few very large values pull the mean up but barely move the median

items.q: What does the standard deviation of a set of data measure?
items.a: How spread out the values are around the mean

items.q: In statistics, how is the variance related to the standard deviation?
items.a: The variance is the standard deviation squared

ideas.title: Probability
ideas.summary: Probability gives each possible outcome a number from 0 to 1, and those numbers obey a few simple rules.

items.q: In probability, what does it mean for two events to be independent?
items.a: Knowing that one happened does not change the probability of the other

items.q: What is the probability of rolling a six twice in a row with a fair six-sided die?
In probability, what is the expected value of a random quantity?
items.a: Its long-run average: each possible value weighted by its probability

items.q: What does the law of large numbers say?
items.a: As the number of trials grows, the average result approaches the expected value

ideas.title: Bayes' theorem
ideas.summary: Bayes' theorem says how much a piece of evidence should change the probability you give to a claim.

items.q: What does the conditional probability P(A|B) mean?
items.a: The probability of A given that B has happened

items.q: What is the formula of Bayes' theorem for P(A|B)?
items.a: P(A|B) = P(B|A) x P(A) / P(B)

items.q: In Bayesian reasoning, what is the probability you give a claim before seeing the evidence called?
items.a: The prior

items.q: What is the error called of ignoring how rare a condition is when judging what a positive test result means?
items.a: Base rate neglect, also called the base rate fallacy

ideas.title: The normal distribution
ideas.summary: Many measurements pile up in a symmetric bell curve fixed by just its mean and standard deviation.

items.q: In a normal distribution, about what share of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean?
items.a: About 68%

items.q: In a normal distribution, about what share of values lie within two standard deviations of the mean?
items.a: About 95%

items.q: Which theorem says that the mean of a large random sample is close to normally distributed, almost whatever the shape of the population?
items.a: The central limit theorem

ideas.title: Sampling and confidence
ideas.summary: A random sample can stand in for a whole population, with an uncertainty that shrinks as the sample grows.

items.q: What is the formula for the standard error of a sample mean, given standard deviation s and sample size n?
items.a: s divided by the square root of n

items.q: To halve the standard error of a sample mean, by what factor must the sample size grow?
items.a: Four times

items.q: In statistics, what is the systematic error called that comes from a sample which does not represent the population?
items.a: Sampling bias

items.q: What does the 95% in a 95% confidence interval refer to?
items.a: If the study were repeated many times, about 95% of such intervals would contain the true value

ideas.title: Significance and causation
ideas.summary: A p-value measures surprise if nothing were going on, and an association alone does not show a cause.

items.q: In a statistical test, what is the null hypothesis?
items.a: The default assumption that there is no effect or no difference

items.q: What does a p-value measure?
items.a: The probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true

items.q: In hypothesis testing, what is a Type I error?
items.a: A false positive: rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true

items.q: In statistics, what is a confounding variable?
items.a: A third factor that affects both variables and makes them look causally linked

items.q: Which study design gives the strongest evidence of cause, because chance alone decides who gets the treatment?
items.a: A randomized controlled trial
